also: it had not entered my mind
that had never occurred to me

evidence: Ter. Eun. 816: Jam dūdum animus est in patinīs.
Cic. Sen. 38: corpore senex esse poterit, animō numquam erit
Traupman 104: quid tibi in animō est?
terms.comment: The mind as the seat of thought and feeling: in animō habēre, to have in mind, intend (see mean, intend); ex animō, from the heart; animum advertere, to notice.

evidence: Cic. Off. 1.105: hominis autem mēns discendō alitur et cōgitandō
Plaut. Amph. 293: Mī in mentem vēnit
terms.comment: The thinking mind: in mentem venīre, to come into one’s head; mente captus, out of one’s mind (Cic. Ac. 2.53, Lewis & Short).

terms.grammar: phrase: what occurs is the subject, the person in the dative
evidence: Plaut. Am. 2.2.34: quid tibi istuc in mentem venit? (Lewis & Short s.v. mēns)
Plaut. Aul. 2.2.49: venit hoc mihi in mentem (Lewis & Short)
Traupman 104: it had not entered my mind, mihi in mentem nōn vēnerat
Traupman 105: that had never occurred to me, mihi istuc numquam in mentem vēnerat
terms.comment: English says “I thought of it”; Latin says “it came into my mind”: mihi in mentem vēnit. With a genitive it means “to remember”: venit mihi Platōnis in mentem is Cicero’s idiom (see remember).
Lewis & Short: in this sense post-Augustan.

phrases.latin: Jam dūdum animus est in patinīs.
phrases.english: My mind has been on the dishes for ages.

phrases.latin: hominis autem mēns discendō alitur et cōgitandō
phrases.english: but the human mind is fed by learning and thinking

phrases.latin: quod quī sequitur, corpore senex esse poterit, animō numquam erit
phrases.english: whoever follows this may be old in body, but will never be old in mind

phrases.latin: Mihi istuc numquam in mentem vēnerat.
phrases.english: That had never occurred to me.
